mekayis.metin: (سَحَّ) السِّينُ وَالْحَاءُ أَصْلٌ وَاحِدٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الصَّبِّ، يُقَالُ سَحَحْتُ [الْمَاءَ] أَسُحُّ سَحًّا. وَسَحَابَةٌ سَحُوحٌ، أَيْ صَبَّابَةٌ. وَشَاةٌ سَاحٌّ، أَيْ سَمِينَةٌ، كَأَنَّهَا تَسُحُّ الْوَدَكَ سَحًّا. وَفَرَسٌ مِسَحٌّ، أَيْ سَرِيعَةٌ يُشْبِهُ عَدْوُهَا انْصِبَابَ الْمَطَرِ. وَيُقَالُ سَحْسَحَ الشَّيْءُ، إِذَا سَالَ. وَيُقَالُ إِنَّ السَّحْسَحَةَ هِيَ السَّاحَةُ.

kaikki_vikisozluk.t: Borrowed from Egyptian sḫt (“field, open country”). Unrelated to سَاحَ (sāḥa, “to travel”) if that sense as opposed to “to run, to melt” is not denominal from the present noun. Compare رِيف (rīf, “countryside, rural land”) also borrowed from Egyptian.
s: Borrowed from Egyptian sḫt (“field, open country”)

kaikki_vikisozluk.e: سَحَّ • (saḥḥa) I (non-past يَسُحُّ (yasuḥḥu), verbal noun سَحّ (saḥḥ) or سُحُوح (suḥūḥ))
g: to pour abundantly or flow forth vehemently and in consecutive quantities (upon)
to flog, to inflict whips on

kaikki_vikisozluk.e: سَحَّ • (saḥḥa) I (non-past يَسِحُّ (yasiḥḥu), verbal noun سَحّ (saḥḥ) or سُحُوح (suḥūḥ) or سُحُوحَة (suḥūḥa))
g: to be fat to the utmost degree (said of bovids)

kaikki_vikisozluk.t: Unknown. Perhaps borrowed from Iranian. Compare Old Armenian ազոխ (azox, “unripe grapes”), Persian ازخ (azox, “rotten and empty nut”).
g: dates or in particular dates that are dry in such a manner that they dissolve well in the mouth

kaikki_vikisozluk.e:
أسح (form I)
# أَسُحُّ (ʔasuḥḥu) /ʔa.suħ.ħu/: first-person singular non-past active indicative of سَحَّ (saḥḥa)
# أُسَحُّ (ʔusaḥḥu) /ʔu.saħ.ħu/: first-person singular non-past passive indicative of سَحَّ (saḥḥa)
# أَسُحَّ (ʔasuḥḥa) /ʔa.suħ.ħa/: first-person singular non-past active subjunctive/jussive of سَحَّ (saḥḥa)
# أُسَحَّ (ʔusaḥḥa) /ʔu.saħ.ħa/: first-person singular non-past passive subjunct
kaikki_vikisozluk.t: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

This could be taken as from the root م س ح (m s ḥ) above as for a wiping rag, however the cloths denoted by this word do not seem to have been adapted for such an employment, and their property of coarseness makes the term adverse to that root’s meanings for smoothness. Therefore a connection to Coptic ⲙⲟϫϩ (mojh, “girdle of a soldier or monk”) or a related word is suggested.
s: Coptic ⲙⲟϫϩ (mojh, “girdle of a soldier or monk”)
g: a coarse cloth, sackcloth, gunny, haircloth
